Field observations of Violet-throated starfrontlet (Coeligena violifer) in the Peruvian cloud forests indicate that freshly laid eggs are incubated under conditions averaging 28 °C [T = 28 °C], with hatching occurring after approximately 18 days [ab = approximately 18 days]. This incubation period is relatively brief compared to many other Andean hummingbirds of similar body mass, likely reflecting the thermoregulatory demands of the high-altitude environment. At the moment of hatching, the altricial nestlings exhibit a minute initial wet weight of only 0.98 grams [Ww0 = 0.98 grams], a value that underscores their extreme dependence on parental provisioning during the first weeks of life. This hatchling mass represents a remarkably small fraction of the ultimate adult body mass, a pattern consistent with the highly altricial developmental mode typical of trochilids, and it sets the stage for a period of extraordinarily rapid growth fueled by frequent regurgitative feedings from the adult female.

As the nestlings develop within the nest, sexual dimorphism in body size becomes increasingly apparent. Adult females of Coeligena violifer attain an ultimate wet weight of approximately 7.0 grams [Wwi = approximately 7.0 grams], while adult males are notably heavier, reaching an ultimate wet weight of 8.1 grams [Wwi = 8.1 grams]. This approximately 15% difference in mass is a common feature among polygynous hummingbird species, where larger male body size is often advantageous in territorial disputes over floral resources and lekking sites. The contrast between the minute hatchling mass and these adult values illustrates the dramatic growth trajectory that must be completed within the brief nestling period. Data from marked individuals suggest that both sexes achieve these asymptotic masses within their first year, with the difference becoming fully expressed after the completion of the post-juvenile molt, a time when feather replacement and skeletal maturation are largely finished.

Under the thermoneutral conditions typically experienced by adults during active foraging periods, which correspond to a body temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C], the species exhibits a maximum basal metabolic rate of 25.45 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 25.45 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This relatively modest metabolic rate, when scaled against the adult body mass, aligns well with predictions for a high-altitude specialist that must conserve energy during cool Andean mornings. At this same body temperature of 38.1 °C, key developmental milestones have been documented in captive-reared individuals. Fledging, defined as the achievement of sustained flight and nest departure, occurs at 23 days after hatching [tx = 23 days after hatching], a relatively early age compared to larger-bodied trochilids at a temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. Shortly thereafter, the attainment of sexual maturity, or puberty, is reached at 69 days after hatching [tp = 69 days after hatching], a remarkably swift pace for a bird of this size that reflects the selective pressures of a short breeding season in the high Andes at a temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C].

The reproductive output of Coeligena violifer is characterized by a conservative strategy that is common among hummingbirds inhabiting seasonal montane environments. Females typically produce a single clutch of exactly two eggs per clutch [N_R_i = two eggs per clutch], with a corresponding clutch frequency of one clutch per year [F_R_i = one clutch per year]. This annual reproductive effort, producing only two offspring per season, is relatively low compared to tropical lowland hummingbirds, which may produce multiple broods within a single year. The small clutch size is likely a direct consequence of the energetic constraints imposed by the demanding altricial rearing process, where the female must assume sole responsibility for incubation and chick provisioning. The time since birth at which a female undertakes her first successful brood has been recorded at 365 days after hatching [tR = 365 days after hatching] when operating at a 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C] body temperature.

Longevity records for Violet-throated starfrontlet in the wild, compiled from banding studies at several long-term monitoring sites in the Cordillera Oriental, indicate that the maximum lifespan is approximately 7.7 years [am = approximately 7.7 years] for individuals operating at a core body temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. This lifespan is impressive for a bird of its size and suggests a relatively slow-paced life history strategy, where high adult survival compensates for the low annual fecundity. The remarkable longevity may be linked to the species' nectarivorous diet, which provides a high-energy but constant foraging challenge, and to the relative safety of its montane cloud forest habitat from many lowland predators. Comparative analyses within the genus Coeligena suggest that such longevity is not exceptional for the group, with several congeneric species also demonstrating lifespans exceeding five years. This combination of a small clutch size, delayed first reproduction until the second calendar year, and extended adult survival aligns well with predictions for a "slow" life history along the fast-slow continuum, a pattern frequently observed in tropical and high-altitude avian species.
